title: {{NAME}} and the Clockwork Garden That Forgot to Bloom
moral: Caring for something small and fragile teaches us more about strength than any great feat.

pages.content:
The Clockwork Garden of Princess Odette had not bloomed in three years. Its mechanical flowers, each petal a sliver of hammered copper or pressed silver, each stem a spiral of fine brass tubing, stood perfectly still in their geometric beds, their clockwork mechanisms wound but inactive, their colours dulled to tarnish. Princess Odette herself was not distressed about this in a dramatic way. She was distressed about it quietly and consistently, the way people are distressed about things they care about deeply and haven't been able to fix.

{{NAME}} arrived at the garden gate carrying a tool bag that clinked pleasantly and a letter of introduction from the Royal Mechanical Institute. The gate itself was a masterpiece: interlocking gears the size of wagon wheels, connected by chains no thicker than a finger, all frozen mid-motion like a stopped clock three years older than anything around it.

And everywhere, in the petals of the silent copper flowers, curled in the cup of a frozen brass lily, perched on the ridges of motionless silver tulips, were fairies. Dozens of them. The size of a thumb, with wings like stained glass and expressions of concentrated concern. They had been living in the garden for the three silent years, {{NAME}} would learn, trying in their small patient way to understand what was wrong. They hadn't given up. They had just run out of ideas.

pages.content:
The robot was the last thing {{NAME}} expected to find in the garden's central pavilion.

Its name was POLLEN-4 and it had been built specifically to tend the Clockwork Garden, its delicate articulated fingers designed to turn the smallest adjustment screws without disturbing a single petal. But something had happened three years ago: a thunderstorm, a power surge, and POLLEN-4 had locked into a loop, turning its fine-fingered hands over and over in a motion that adjusted nothing, fixed nothing, but couldn't stop.

Odette watched from the pavilion doorway with the careful expression of someone managing sadness they've had a long time. 'I didn't want to switch it off,' she said, quietly. 'It tried so hard.' The fairies had clustered on POLLEN-4's shoulders and in the curl of its hair-thin antennae, keeping it company for three years in their small, faithful way.

{{NAME}} crouched at POLLEN-4's level and looked at the looping hands. Not a mechanical failure. The gears were intact. This was a software loop: the robot's intent remained but its path to the action had been severed by the surge. POLLEN-4 still wanted to tend the garden. It had never stopped wanting to.

{{NAME}}'s eyes went from the robot's searching hands to the tarnished flowers. There was something enormously patient about both of them. Something that deserved a solution.

pages.content:
The repair took all afternoon and required the smallest screwdriver in {{NAME}}'s kit, seventeen fairies acting as extra hands to hold microscopic components steady, and Odette's own precise and steady fingers for the final calibration, because her touch with the mechanical flowers, developed over years of learning their temperament, was finer than any tool.

The fairies were extraordinary. They could feel the vibration frequency of a gear through their wing-tips and signal with colour changes when something was correctly aligned. Teal for true. Red for wrong. Pale yellow for close but not quite. They worked without ego and without impatience, clustering around the most difficult junctions with the dedicated energy of creatures for whom something important has been sitting broken for too long.

{{NAME}} ran the new pathway code into POLLEN-4's core system from the portable programmer, fingers steady, watching the progress indicator with the kind of attention that had no room for anything else. Odette held her breath so quietly it was almost like not breathing at all.

POLLEN-4's hands stopped looping. A pause, the absolute mechanical stillness of a system reorienting itself. Then the fingers opened, spread, and reached with intention toward the nearest copper rose. Odette made a sound so small it was more of a shape of breath than a sound. Three fairies performed instant aerial somersaults. {{NAME}} let out a breath that had apparently been held for quite some time.

pages.content:
POLLEN-4 made one quarter-turn on the first copper rose's central gear, a movement no bigger than a coin's rotation, and the whole garden responded.

It started with a sound: a soft, cascading tick-tick-tick-tick that spread outward from the pavilion like a musical rumour, flower to flower, bed to bed. Then the motion: petals unfurling in a copper wave, silver tulips lifting their heads, brass lilies opening petal by petal with the slow ceremony of something that has been waiting to do this for three years and intends to do it properly. The tarnish caught the afternoon light and turned, not to silver, but to gold.

The fairies rose as one, a cloud of stained-glass wings and delighted colour, their collective sound a high, harmonious chime that had no human equivalent but translated perfectly in the chest. They moved through the blooming garden like a flock of tiny joyous birds, alighting on each opened flower, checking each mechanism with their wing-tip sensors, cataloguing the new bloom with the thoroughness of people who know the value of what they've been waiting for.

Odette stood at the garden's centre with the afternoon light turning her gown from blue to gold, and her face did the complicated thing that faces do when a very old hope becomes a very present fact. POLLEN-4 moved along the first row with the purposeful grace of a creature finally doing the exact thing it was made to do.

pages.content:
By evening, every flower in the Clockwork Garden was open and moving in the slight breeze in the way of things both mechanical and alive. The tick-tick of their mechanisms had settled into a steady rhythm that was, if you sat quietly enough to hear it properly, remarkably like a heartbeat.

The fairies were everywhere, nested in the open blooms, draped in the brass lily cups, riding the copper rose petals with the ease of creatures who had finally come home to themselves. One particularly small fairy sat directly on {{NAME}}'s knee and fell asleep within thirty seconds, which was the greatest compliment {{NAME}} had ever been paid.

POLLEN-4 had completed two full circuits of the garden by now and sat in the pavilion with the patient readiness of a gardener who has finished today's work and is thinking about tomorrow's. Odette sat on the bench beside {{NAME}} with the sleeping fairy between them and said nothing for a long while. Then, 'It was never really about the flowers.' {{NAME}} understood what she meant. It was about not giving up on something you love.

The clockwork tick spread through the cool evening air like a lullaby that someone built instead of sang. Close your eyes, dear one, and let it count your breaths toward sleep. And in the garden tonight, in the deepest flower, a fairy is dreaming of a room the garden hasn't opened yet.
